title: Canadian ‘gauntlets’ to turn drone procurement into live competitions
html:
Chaac Technologies demonstrates SHIELDS, which detects mines using machine learning, on a Freefly drone during GCXpo 2026, a demonstration showcase of Canadian next-gen tech, at Area X.O in Ottawa, on Sept. 29.Justin Tang/The Canadian Press

Ottawa is launching a series of live drone procurement competitions across the country as it seeks to bolster the marketplace of domestic suppliers for the technologies, mirroring a US$1-billion initiative launched by U.S. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last year.

Canada’s “gauntlets,” as they’re called in the U.S., will be field trials used to evaluate certain drone and counterdrone technology on the spot, expediting the procurement of low-cost systems for the Canadian Armed Forces.

They will be run through Ottawa’s Defence Drone Initiative, which launched in July and is set to receive $2.3-billion over five years, beginning next fiscal year, according to the 2026 federal budget.

The initiative aims to foster a domestic supply chain for drones, as well as their components, and is part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s effort to build a sovereign defence industry. It could also help create opportunities for companies to test at home rather than travel elsewhere to trial their technologies.

The live drone contests will likely take place over the course of a week, during which companies bidding for a specific contract will come together at a testing facility to have their products trialled by Canadian Armed Forces members and ranked based upon their performance, said Lieutenant-Colonel Nick Verreault, head of the Forces’ Joint Uncrewed Systems Office.

Contracts will then be awarded based upon the resulting leaderboard. Lt.-Col. Verreault said this is the federal government’s way of optimizing how it runs trials and bid evaluations, by relying more heavily on industry for testing opportunities.

“We’re trying to be more streamlined in our approach,” he said.

However, he added that the competitive process is still being fine-tuned and is subject to changes when the Defence Investment Agency puts out bid solicitations in the new year.

The U.S. launched its version of these challenges, called Drone Dominance, in December 2025, with the aim of expediting the growth of its industrial base and arming its military with “consumable drones at scale,” according to the program’s website.

Since then, it has held two gauntlets, or live competitions, focused on various drone capabilities, such as fighting in confined environments and long-range strikes. After each challenge, the top 10 companies, at least, have each received orders for thousands of drones from the U.S. government.

The initiative has attracted interest from dozens of companies, including the U.S. subsidiaries of Canadian drone companies Volatus Aerospace and Draganfly Inc. The qualifying round for the program’s second challenge, for example, featured 49 companies and put 79 different drones to the test, according to its website.

Canada’s gauntlets are not yet so advanced, despite the federal government’s stated goal to produce two million drones per year.

First, Ottawa must identify the facilities where its version of these challenges can take place. This will be done through its Defence Drone Initiative, which includes a stream for companies that can facilitate testing, evaluation and training. In the new year, a request for proposals will go out to qualified vendors in this stream to host the forthcoming challenges.

“Think of it as a service contract where vendors will be asked to book a site, book the airspace, build a test plan, have it validated by CAF to make sure that it meets the mandatory and rated criteria as part of the contract, and subsequently execute the bid evaluation with CAF members present,” Lt.-Col. Verreault said.

The Armed Forces members are the deciding authority in terms of evaluating companies’ products. However, Lt.-Col. Verreault added that it will be important for the vendor running the challenge not to be affiliated with any of the participating companies.

The format of the contracts sought through these challenges will vary and could come in the form of standing offers or direct commercial sales, for example. But a field trial will be at the heart of all of them. To start, Lt.-Col. Verreault said the CAF will be running gauntlets for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, as well as strike drones with first-person view, meaning a remote pilot can see where they’re flying.

These gauntlets prod at a broader issue plaguing defence companies in Canada around testing opportunities. Kath Intson and Niru Somayajula, both chief executive officers of drone and sensor companies, respectively, told The Globe and Mail in October that their struggle to find places to test their technologies in Canada has often led them to go to other countries, such as the U.S., for trials.

The surging demand from industry to test in specific environments, such as electronic warfare conditions, is placing stress upon the federal government to find a solution, or risk either sending companies elsewhere or slowing their progress as they wait to access facilities in Canada.

Lt.-Col. Verreault said part of the aim of launching gauntlet-style challenges in Canada, in collaboration with industry, is to reduce some of that stress, in particular in places like Canadian Forces Base Suffield, which the military and industry rely upon for a broad swath of testing, including explosives, for example.

On the one hand, identifying and incentivizing more civilian testing facilities across Canada could lessen the load on military bases for straightforward trials like flight tests. On the other hand, Lt.-Col. Verreault said he’s also hoping to identify more areas where complex electronic-warfare tests can legally take place.

Once a pool of suitable gauntlet vendors has been established, a call for services will go out to these providers every time the federal government wants to host a field trial.

By the time the request for proposals to join this pool is posted in the new year, Ottawa’s drone marketplace will have grown in size. The federal government is opening up applications to join the marketplace of prequalified suppliers every three months for its first year.

Its initial round of applications closed over the summer and led to the acceptance of nearly 400 suppliers who can now bid on subsequent contracts released to the marketplace.

The second round closed at the beginning of November. Lt.-Col. Verreault said 208 applications have been received and an announcement of how many were accepted is expected in the coming weeks.
summary: Ottawa’s Defence Drone Initiative aims to establish marketplace of suppliers, provide opportunities for them to test their hardware
